definition: Best-first search that expands the node with the lowest f(n) = g(n) + h(n), path cost so far plus heuristic estimate. Optimal with an admissible (tree search) or consistent (graph search) heuristic.
Non-linear function applied to a neuron's weighted input, e.g. ReLU, sigmoid, tanh, GELU. Without it, stacked layers collapse into one linear map.

Optimiser that keeps running averages of gradients (momentum) and squared gradients, and scales each parameter's step accordingly. With decoupled weight decay (AdamW) it is the standard for training Transformers.
A heuristic that never overestimates the true cost to reach a goal: h(n) ≤ h*(n). Guarantees that A* tree search finds an optimal solution.
Anything that perceives its environment through sensors and acts on it through actuators.
The abstract mapping from percept sequences to actions that describes an agent's behaviour; implemented concretely by an agent program.
A period of reduced funding and interest in AI after inflated expectations were not met; notably the mid-1970s and the late 1980s to early 1990s.
The problem of making an AI system pursue the goals its designers and users actually intend, rather than a flawed proxy for them.
Optimisation of minimax that skips branches which cannot affect the final decision. Same result as minimax; with perfect move ordering it examines about b^(m/2) nodes instead of b^m.
In a CSP, the arc X → Y is consistent if every value of X has some compatible value of Y. The AC-3 algorithm removes values until all arcs are consistent.
The study and construction of agents that act rationally, i.e. that choose actions expected to maximise a performance measure. Other definitions emphasise human-like thought or behaviour.
Mechanism that computes a weighted average of value vectors, with weights given by the softmax of query–key similarities. Lets each position draw information directly from any other position.
Computing exact derivatives of a program by recording its elementary operations and applying the chain rule to them. Reverse-mode autodiff is backpropagation; PyTorch and JAX implement it.
Algorithm that computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight of a network in one backward pass, by applying the chain rule layer by layer.
Depth-first search for CSPs that assigns one variable at a time and backs up as soon as a constraint is violated.
Directed acyclic graph of random variables with a conditional probability table per node; compactly represents a joint distribution as the product of P(X | parents(X)).
Recursive equation for value functions: the value of a state equals the expected immediate reward plus the discounted value of the successor state, under the best (optimality form) or a given policy.
A standard dataset and metric for comparing models, e.g. MMLU, GSM8K, SWE-bench.
Uninformed search that expands the shallowest unexpanded node first (FIFO queue). Complete; optimal for equal step costs; O(b^d) time and memory.
Systematic unfair differences in a model's behaviour across groups of people, inherited from data, labels, proxy features or problem framing.
Decomposition of expected test error into bias (error from wrong assumptions), variance (sensitivity to the training sample) and noise. More flexible models trade lower bias for higher variance.
Tokenisation algorithm that starts with single bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token, until the vocabulary reaches a target size.
Attention mask that prevents each position from attending to later positions, by setting their scores to −∞. Used in decoder-only language models.
Intermediate reasoning steps a model writes out before its final answer. Reasoning models are trained with reinforcement learning to produce long chains of thought.
Splitting documents into passages (chunks) for retrieval, typically a few hundred tokens long with some overlap.
A logical sentence written as a conjunction (AND) of clauses, each a disjunction (OR) of literals. Every propositional sentence has an equivalent CNF.
Network that applies small learned filters across a grid input with shared weights, exploiting locality and translation invariance. The standard architecture for images before vision Transformers.
A search algorithm is complete if it is guaranteed to find a solution whenever one exists.
P(A | B) = P(A, B) / P(B): the probability of A given that B is known to be true.
Benchmark test items appearing in a model's training data, which inflates its scores.
The maximum number of tokens a language model can take into account at once: prompt, conversation history and its own output together.
cos(u, v) = u·v / (‖u‖‖v‖); similarity of two vectors' directions, from −1 to 1. The standard measure for comparing embeddings.
Loss −log p̂(y): the negative log-probability the model assigns to the correct class or token. Minimising it is maximum likelihood estimation.
Evaluation scheme that splits data into k folds, trains k times on k−1 folds and tests on the held-out fold, then averages the results.
Problem defined by variables, their domains and constraints on combinations of values; a solution assigns every variable a value satisfying all constraints.
The token-by-token generation phase of LLM inference. Each step reads all weights from memory, so speed is limited by memory bandwidth.
Machine learning with neural networks of many layers that learn their own feature representations from raw data.
Uninformed search that expands the deepest node first (stack). Needs only O(bm) memory but is neither complete nor optimal in general.
Alignment method that fine-tunes a model directly on pairs of preferred and rejected responses, without training a separate reward model.
Regularisation technique that randomly sets a fraction of activations to zero during training.
A dense vector representation of a discrete item (token, word, sentence, image), learned so that similar items have nearby vectors.
KB ⊨ α: α is true in every model in which the knowledge base KB is true.
One complete pass over the training data.
Training principle: choose the parameters that minimise the average loss over the training examples.
Function that estimates the utility of a non-terminal game position, used when search is cut off at a depth limit.
Rule-based program encoding a human expert's knowledge as if-then rules; the dominant AI technology of the 1980s.
The trade-off between choosing the best-known action (exploit) and trying others that might be better (explore).
Continuing to train a pre-trained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset.
Logic with objects, predicates, functions and the quantifiers ∀ and ∃; far more expressive than propositional logic, but entailment is only semi-decidable.
The set of nodes generated but not yet expanded during search. Search strategies differ in which frontier node they expand next.
File format of llama.cpp (and LM Studio) for storing model weights, usually quantised, together with tokenizer and metadata.
Vector of partial derivatives of a function with respect to each parameter; points in the direction of steepest increase.
Optimisation by repeatedly stepping against the gradient: θ ← θ − η∇L(θ).
Fluent, confident model output that is false or unsupported by the input.
A function h(n) estimating the cost of the cheapest path from a node to a goal, used to guide informed search.
A setting chosen before training rather than learned, e.g. learning rate, batch size, number of layers, regularisation strength.
Repeated depth-limited DFS with increasing limits. Complete and optimal for unit costs with only O(bd) memory.
An LLM's ability to perform a task from instructions or examples given in the prompt, without any weight updates.
A and B are independent if P(A, B) = P(A)P(B); conditionally independent given C if P(A, B | C) = P(A | C)P(B | C).
The assumptions a learning method builds in, which determine how it generalises beyond its training data, e.g. locality in CNNs.
In logic: deriving new sentences from a knowledge base. In machine learning, also: running a trained model to make predictions.
A prompt crafted to make a model bypass its safety training and produce output it would normally refuse.
The probability of every combination of values of a set of random variables.
A set of sentences in a formal language representing what an agent knows.
A large store of facts as subject–predicate–object triples connecting entities, e.g. Wikidata.
Stored attention keys and values of all previous tokens, so that each generation step only computes them for the new token. Grows linearly with context length.
Step size η in gradient descent; usually the most important hyperparameter.
P(E | H): the probability of the observed evidence under a hypothesis, viewed as a function of the hypothesis or parameters.
A Transformer with billions of parameters trained on next-token prediction over very large text corpora, usually followed by instruction tuning and preference optimisation.
A system that runs a language model in a loop, letting it call tools, observe results and act until a task is done.
Linear classifier that maps a weighted sum of features through the sigmoid function to a probability.
The raw, unnormalised scores a model outputs for each class or token, before the softmax turns them into probabilities.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning that freezes the model and learns small low-rank update matrices for selected weight matrices.
Function measuring how wrong a prediction is; training minimises its average over the data.
Recurrent network unit with a cell state and gates controlling what to keep, forget and output; remembers over much longer spans than a plain RNN.
Methods that improve at a task from data or experience instead of being explicitly programmed.
Game-tree search that estimates move values from many simulated playouts and grows the tree towards promising moves, balancing exploration and exploitation.
Formal model of sequential decisions: states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards and a discount factor, with the Markov property.
A small random subset of the training data used to estimate the gradient for one update step.
Decision rule for two-player zero-sum games: MAX picks the move with the highest value assuming MIN always replies with the move of lowest value.
Choosing the parameters that make the observed data most probable. MAP estimation additionally multiplies by a prior.
Feed-forward neural network of fully connected layers with non-linear activations between them.
Architecture where a router sends each token to a few of many expert sub-networks, so only a fraction of the parameters is used per token.
Several attention operations run in parallel on separate learned projections, with their outputs concatenated; lets the model capture several kinds of relations at once.
Classifier that assumes features are conditionally independent given the class: P(C | x) ∝ P(C)∏P(xᵢ | C).
A model composed of layers of simple units (weighted sum plus non-linearity), trained by gradient descent.
Layer that rescales activations to a standard mean and variance (batch norm, layer norm) or root mean square (RMSNorm), stabilising deep-network training.
A formal specification of the concepts in a domain and the relations between them.
A search algorithm is optimal if the solution it returns has the lowest path cost among all solutions.
Fitting the training data, including its noise, so closely that performance on new data suffers.
A value learned during training, e.g. a weight or bias. Model sizes such as "27B" count parameters.
Task description by Performance measure, Environment, Actuators and Sensors.
The complete history of everything an agent has perceived.
Rosenblatt's single artificial neuron with a step activation (1958); learns any linearly separable classification but not XOR.
The criterion that defines success for an agent's behaviour.
exp of the average cross-entropy per token; the effective number of choices a language model is uncertain between. Lower is better.
A mapping from states to actions, or to probability distributions over actions.
Reinforcement learning by gradient ascent on expected return with respect to the policy's parameters; PPO and GRPO are examples.
Information about token order added to a Transformer's input or attention, e.g. sinusoids or rotary position embeddings (RoPE).
P(H | E): the probability of a hypothesis after taking the evidence into account.
Precision: share of predicted positives that are correct. Recall: share of actual positives that are found. F1 is their harmonic mean.
The first phase of LLM inference, which processes the whole prompt in parallel and fills the KV cache; limited by compute.
Self-supervised training of a model on a very large general corpus, e.g. next-token prediction on web text, before any task-specific training.
P(H): the probability of a hypothesis before seeing the evidence.
The input text given to a language model, including any system instructions, conversation history and tool results.
An attack in which instructions hidden in data the model processes (web pages, files, tool output) are followed as if they came from the user.
Model-free reinforcement learning that updates action-value estimates towards r + γ maxₐ′ Q(s′, a′) after each transition.
The three learned projections of each position in attention: the query is matched against keys to weight the values.
Storing model weights (and sometimes activations or the KV cache) with fewer bits, e.g. 4 instead of 16, to save memory and bandwidth.
Answering by first retrieving relevant documents and adding them to the model's prompt.
An agent that, for each percept sequence, chooses the action expected to maximise its performance measure given its evidence and knowledge.
An LLM trained, usually with reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks, to produce an extended chain of thought before answering.
Any technique that reduces overfitting by preferring simpler models, e.g. weight decay, dropout, early stopping, data augmentation.
A version of a problem with fewer constraints; the cost of its optimal solution is an admissible heuristic for the original.
Activation function max(0, z).
Skip connection that adds a block's input to its output, h + F(h); lets gradients flow through very deep networks.
Inference rule combining two clauses with complementary literals into one; refutation-complete for propositional logic.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: train a reward model on human preference comparisons, then optimise the language model against it.
Network that processes a sequence step by step, carrying a hidden state from each step to the next.
Empirical power laws relating model loss to parameter count, training data and compute.
States, initial state, actions, transition model, goal test and action costs; a solution is an action sequence from the initial state to a goal.
Tree of paths explored from the initial state during search; nodes correspond to paths, not to unique states.
Attention in which queries, keys and values all come from the same sequence.
Learning from labels derived automatically from the data itself, e.g. predicting the next token or a masked part of the input.
Fine-tuning a pre-trained model on curated input–output examples, e.g. instruction–response conversations.
Gradient descent using gradient estimates from random mini-batches instead of the full dataset.
Function turning a vector of scores into a probability distribution: softmax(z)ₖ = e^{zₖ} / Σⱼ e^{zⱼ}.
An inference procedure is sound if everything it derives is entailed by the knowledge base.
An agent satisfying the literal objective it was given in an unintended way; also called reward hacking.
The set of all states reachable from the initial state, as a graph whose edges are actions.
A separate agent loop with its own context, started by a main agent for a sub-task; returns only its result.
Learning a function from input–output pairs; classification for categorical outputs, regression for numeric ones.
Sampling parameter that divides logits before the softmax: below 1 makes output more deterministic, above 1 more random.
Held-out data used once, at the end, to estimate a model's performance on unseen data.
The unit of text an LLM reads and writes: a word, word piece, character or byte sequence from its vocabulary.
A model emitting structured calls to external functions, described by name, description and JSON Schema, which the application executes.
Sampling only from the smallest set of tokens whose total probability reaches p.
Neural architecture built from stacked blocks of self-attention and position-wise feed-forward networks with residual connections and normalisation (Vaswani et al., 2017).
Description of the result of each action in each state; deterministic Result(s, a) or probabilistic P(s′ | s, a).
Turing's 1950 "imitation game": a machine passes if a human interrogator cannot reliably tell it from a human in text conversation.
Uninformed search that expands the node with the lowest path cost g(n); Dijkstra's algorithm. Complete and optimal for positive costs.
A model too simple to capture the patterns in the data; both training and test error are high.
A network with one hidden layer and enough units can approximate any continuous function on a bounded domain to any accuracy.
Finding structure in data without labels, e.g. clustering, dimensionality reduction, density estimation.
A numeric measure of how desirable a state or outcome is for an agent.
Held-out data used during development to choose hyperparameters and compare models, kept separate from the test set.
V(s): the expected return from state s under a policy; Q(s, a) is the same after first taking action a.
Store for embedding vectors that supports fast (approximate) nearest-neighbour search.
The fixed set of tokens a language model can read and produce, typically 32,000 to 256,000 entries.
